inuit_tekkeitsertok.name: owns the caribou herds and grants or withholds them from the hunter
inuit_tekkeitsertok.notes: As the chief of the land-game spirits in Boas's Central Eskimo / Baffin Land record, he keeps the caribou and only those he releases may be taken; offended, he withholds the herds and the hunt fails.

sources.reference: Franz Boas, The Central Eskimo (1888)

ipisowaahs.name: rises before the dawn as the Morning Star, herald of the Sun
ipisowaahs.notes: Apisirahts / Iipisowaahs, son of Natosi (Sun) and Ko'komiki'somm (Moon), travels the sky as the bright morning planet preceding his father the Sun.

sources.reference: George Bird Grinnell, Blackfoot Lodge Tales (1892), 'The Story of Poia / Scarface'

irish_aengus.name: wins the Brú na Bóinne forever by the riddle of 'a day and a night'
irish_aengus.notes: Aengus asks Elcmar (or the Dagda) for the Brug for la ocus aidche ('a day and a night'); since all time is made of days and nights, he claims it in perpetuity. Tochmarc Étaíne, Dindshenchas.

sources.reference: Tochmarc Étaíne (The Wooing of Étaín)

irish_aengus.name: seeks his dream-love Caer Ibormeith and joins her as a swan
irish_aengus.notes: In Aislinge Óenguso (The Dream of Óengus) he wastes with love for a maiden seen in dreams, finds her among 150 swans chained in pairs at Loch Bél Dracon, and at Samain turns into a swan to be with her.

sources.reference: Aislinge Óenguso (The Dream of Óengus)

irish_aife.name: the fiercest warrior-woman of the western world, rival of Scáthach
irish_aife.notes: Called by Scáthach the hardest woman-warrior in the world; she alone Scáthach feared. Cú Chulainn overcomes her only by a ruse (crying out that her chariot-horses and charioteer have fallen over a cliff). Tochmarc Emire.

sources.reference: Tochmarc Emire (The Wooing of Emer)

irish_balor.name: slays Nuada Airgetlám in the Second Battle of Mag Tuired before Lugh fells him
irish_balor.notes: Cath Maige Tuired: Balor kills King Nuada (and Macha) on the field; his death-eye is then pierced by Lugh's sling-stone so that it falls back through his own host.

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

irish_boann.name: her transgression of the Well of Segais looses the river and the waters of wisdom
irish_boann.notes: Metrical Dindshenchas of Boand: she walks left-handwise (tuathal) round the forbidden Well of Segais (Nechtan's well, ringed by the nine hazels of wisdom); the well rises, maims and drowns her, and pursues her to the sea as the Boyne.

sources.reference: Metrical Dindshenchas, 'Boand I'

irish_brigid.name: presides over filidecht (poetry), healing and smithwork as a triple goddess
irish_brigid.notes: Cormac's Glossary (Sanas Cormaic) makes Brigit a goddess worshipped by poets, with two sisters of the same name, one over leechcraft (healing) and one over smithwork — the threefold patroness of fili, leech and smith.

sources.reference: Sanas Cormaic (Cormac's Glossary), s.v. Brigit

irish_cian.name: turns himself into a pig to escape the sons of Tuireann
irish_cian.notes: Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann: pursued by Brian, Iuchar and Iucharba, Cian changes into a pig and mixes with a herd; they wound him as a pig, and he is allowed to die in human form, his blood crying out for vengeance.

sources.reference: Oidheadh Chloinne Tuireann (The Fate of the Children of Tuireann)

irish_dian_cecht.name: fashions a working silver arm for the maimed King Nuada
irish_dian_cecht.notes: After Nuada loses his hand at the First Battle of Mag Tuired, Dian Cécht makes him a silver arm with full movement of every joint and finger (later bettered by his son Miach, who grows skin and flesh over it).

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

irish_dian_cecht.name: raises the slain whole again through the Well of Sláine
irish_dian_cecht.notes: He and his children Octriuil, Miach and Airmed chant spells over the well Tipra Sláine, into which the mortally wounded are cast and emerge living and whole, so the Tuatha Dé seem an inexhaustible host.

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

irish_goibniu.name: forges a finished spear-head with three blows of the hammer
irish_goibniu.notes: With Luchta the wright and Creidne the brazier, Goibniu re-makes the Tuatha Dé's broken weapons each night of the battle: he beats out a spear-head in three strokes so that every spear is whole by morning. Cath Maige Tuired.

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

irish_lir.name: ancestral sea-lord whose four children are bound 900 years as swans
irish_lir.notes: Oidheadh Chloinne Lir: passed over for the kingship of the sídhe in favour of Bodb Derg, Lir is reconciled and given Bodb's daughter Aobh; her sons and daughter Fionnuala are cursed into swan-form by his second wife Aoife for 900 years.

sources.reference: Oidheadh Chloinne Lir (The Fate of the Children of Lir)

irish_eriu.name: greets the invading Milesians and prophesies the land will be theirs forever
irish_eriu.notes: Lebor Gabála Érenn: when Ériu meets the Sons of Míl at Uisneach she foretells that the island will belong to them to the world's end, asking only that it bear her name; Amergin grants it.

sources.reference: Lebor Gabála Érenn (The Book of the Taking of Ireland)

irish_donn.name: raises storms and sickness from Tech Duinn against the living
irish_donn.notes: In later folklore Donn Fírinne / Donn of the dead is said to ride the storm-clouds and send tempests and cattle-disease; the dead pass to his house, and seeing him portends death.

sources.reference: Dáithí Ó hÓgáin, Myth, Legend and Romance: An Encyclopaedia of the Irish Folk Tradition (1990), s.v. Donn

irish_midir.name: wins back Étaín from King Eochaid by staking her at fidchell
irish_midir.notes: Tochmarc Étaíne: Midir loses game after game to Eochaid (paying horses, cauldrons, and great works of land-clearing), then for the last stake wins a kiss and embrace of Étaín, seizes her, and the pair rise through the skylight as two swans joined by a golden chain.

sources.reference: Tochmarc Étaíne (The Wooing of Étaín)

irish_medb.name: confers the kingship of Connacht; no man may be king at Crúachan but her husband
irish_medb.notes: As a sovereignty figure (identified with Medb Lethderg of Tara), the king rules only through union with her; she chose Ailill as a man without meanness, jealousy or fear, and is said to have been wedded to nine kings of Ireland.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_medb.name: musters and commands the four provinces of Ireland in the cattle-raid
irish_medb.notes: Medb is the driving will of the Táin: provoked by the pillow-talk reckoning of property, she raises the army of Connacht and its allies to seize the Donn Cúailnge from Ulster.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_scathach.name: teaches the warrior-feats (cless), the salmon-leap and the hero's craft of arms
irish_scathach.notes: On her island in Alba she trains Cú Chulainn (and Ferdiad) in the full repertoire of feats — the salmon-leap, the apple-feat, the thunder-feat, the rope-feat and the rest. Tochmarc Emire.

sources.reference: Tochmarc Emire (The Wooing of Emer)

irish_scathach.name: prophesies Cú Chulainn's destiny through the imbas forosnai (the great knowledge that illumines)
irish_scathach.notes: Scáthach foretells in verse (the 'Verba Scáthaige') the deeds and combats that await Cú Chulainn on the Táin, and warns of his short, glorious life.

sources.reference: Verba Scáthaige (The Words of Scáthach)

irish_tailtiu.name: clears the wood of Cúan into the open plain of Brega, dying of the labour
irish_tailtiu.notes: Metrical Dindshenchas of Tailtiu: the Fir Bolg queen fells the great forest into arable plain; the toil kills her, and with her dying breath she asks that funeral games be held at Lughnasa in her name.

sources.reference: Metrical Dindshenchas, 'Tailtiu'

irish_fand.name: summons Cú Chulainn to the Otherworld as bird-woman and lover
irish_fand.notes: Serglige Con Culainn: Fand and her sister Lí Ban appear as enchanted birds linked by a silver chain; she lays Cú Chulainn low with whips in a vision, then through Lí Ban offers herself and aid in war against Labraid's enemies in Mag Mell.

sources.reference: Serglige Con Culainn (The Wasting-Sickness of Cú Chulainn)

irish_ailill.name: matches his wealth against Medb's in the pillow-talk that opens the Táin
irish_ailill.notes: Táin Bó Cúailnge: the comparison of their possessions finds them equal but for the bull Finnbhennach, which had quit Medb's herds for Ailill's — the lack that drives Medb to seek the Donn Cúailnge.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_conchobar.name: dies when the embedded brain-ball of Mes Gegra bursts from his skull
irish_conchobar.notes: Aided Chonchobuir: the calcified brain of Mes Gegra, slung into his head by Cet mac Mágach, stays lodged for years; he bursts it in rage on learning of Christ's crucifixion and dies, reckoned a believer.

sources.reference: Aided Chonchobuir (The Death of Conchobar)

irish_sualtam.name: his severed head keeps crying the war-alarm until Ulster wakes
irish_sualtam.notes: Táin Bó Cúailnge: riding to rouse the cursed Ulstermen, Sualtam is beheaded by the rim of his own shield as his horse rears; the head, set on the shield, goes on shouting 'Men are slain, women stolen, cattle driven off!' until Cathbad heeds it.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_fergus.name: shears the tops off three hills with a single stroke of Caladbolg
irish_fergus.notes: Táin Bó Cúailnge: when Cú Chulainn yields to him in single combat by an earlier pact, Fergus turns aside and lops the tops from the three Máela of Meath with the great sword Caladbolg, which makes a stroke like a rainbow.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_connla.name: bound by three geasa never to yield, never to refuse combat, never to tell his name
irish_connla.notes: Aided Óenfhir Aífe: under his father's prohibitions Connla will not name himself even to Cú Chulainn, who is thus driven to fight and kill his own son with the Gáe Bulg before learning who he is.

sources.reference: Aided Óenfhir Aífe (The Death of Aífe's Only Son)

iroquois_atotarho.name: a sorcerer whose hair writhes with snakes and whose body is twisted into seven crooks
iroquois_atotarho.notes: Haudenosaunee tradition: the Onondaga wizard Tadodaho is so malign that serpents grow from his hair and his body bends in seven places; he kills by thought and blocks the peace until Hayowentha combs out the snakes and Deganawida straightens his body with wampum and herbs.

sources.reference: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, The Great Law of Peace (Kaianerekowa)

iroquois_deganawida.name: brings the Great Law of Peace and binds the Five Nations into one Confederacy
iroquois_deganawida.notes: The Peacemaker carries the Kaianerekowa from nation to nation, plants the Great Tree of Peace at Onondaga, and unites the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca under one council fire.

sources.reference: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, The Great Law of Peace (Kaianerekowa)

iroquois_deganawida.name: founds the Condolence rite, clearing grief from the mind with strings of wampum
iroquois_deganawida.notes: He wipes the tears, clears the throat and unstops the ears of the grieving Hayowentha with wampum, instituting the Condolence Ceremony that still raises up new chiefs.

sources.reference: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, The Condolence Ceremony

irish_emer.name: possesses the six gifts of womanhood: beauty, voice, sweet speech, needlework, wisdom and chastity
irish_emer.notes: Tochmarc Emire names Emer as the only woman fit for Cú Chulainn because she holds the six gifts; he woos her through a contest of riddling, cryptic speech.

sources.reference: Tochmarc Emire (The Wooing of Emer)

irish_ferdiad.name: bears a horn-skin (conganchnes) that no point or edge can pierce
irish_ferdiad.notes: Táin Bó Cúailnge: Ferdiad equals Cú Chulainn in every feat save two — Cú Chulainn alone has the Gáe Bulg, and Ferdiad alone has the impenetrable horn-skin, which is why Cú Chulainn must resort to the Gáe Bulg from below the water to kill him.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_findabair.name: offered in marriage, again and again, as the bait to send champions against Cú Chulainn
irish_findabair.notes: Táin Bó Cúailnge: Medb and Ailill promise their daughter's hand to one warrior after another to lure them into facing Cú Chulainn; when the deception is exposed she dies of shame (or, in one telling, for love of Fráech).

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

irish_bodb_derg.name: elected king over the Tuatha Dé Danann of the sídhe after they withdraw underground
irish_bodb_derg.notes: Oidheadh Chloinne Lir / Mythological Cycle: when the Tuath Dé retire into the hollow hills, Bodb Derg son of the Dagda is chosen king of the sídhe over Lir, who is reconciled to him by the gift of his foster-daughter Aobh.

sources.reference: Oidheadh Chloinne Lir (The Fate of the Children of Lir)

iroquois_handsome_lake.name: receives the Gaiwiio (Good Word) from four heavenly messengers in a trance
iroquois_handsome_lake.notes: Stricken in 1799 after years of drink, Ganyodaiyo' falls as if dead and is shown a vision by four (or three) messengers of the Creator; recovering, he preaches a code against alcohol, witchcraft, abortion and quarrelling and renews the old thanksgiving ceremonies.

sources.reference: Arthur C. Parker, The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913)

ipisowaahs.name: the raven feathers and magpie-feather plume the Morning Star gives his son

sources.reference: George Bird Grinnell, Blackfoot Lodge Tales (1892), 'Scarface'

irish_aengus.name: a harp of gold whose music draws all who hear it to follow

sources.reference: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998), s.v. Óengus

irish_aengus.name: Moralltach, the Great Fury, the sword he lends to Diarmuid

sources.reference: Tóraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne (The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Gráinne)

irish_balor.name: the destroying eye, lidded and raised on its ring by four (or nine) attendants

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

irish_dian_cecht.name: the jointed silver arm (Airgetlám) he makes for Nuada

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

irish_eriu.name: the cup of red liquor she presses on the kings, later poured as drunken sovereignty

sources.reference: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998), s.v. Ériu

irish_medb.name: her pet bird and pet squirrel that perch on her shoulders, killed by Cú Chulainn's slingshots

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)

sources.reference: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, The Great Law of Peace (Kaianerekowa)

ipisowaahs.name: the Sun Dance (Okan / Medicine Lodge), kept by the Blackfoot in fulfilment of the Morning Star story
ipisowaahs.notes: The origin-myth of Morning Star, Sun and the youth Poia/Scarface is the charter of the Blackfoot Sun Dance: Scarface returns from the sky-lodge of Sun and Morning Star bearing the rites by which the people honour the Sun each summer.

sources.reference: George Bird Grinnell, Blackfoot Lodge Tales (1892), 'The Story of Poia'

irish_lugh.name: Lughnasadh / Áenach Tailten, the harvest assembly and funeral games Lugh founded for Tailtiu
irish_lugh.notes: Lugh institutes the óenach at Tailtiu in mourning for his foster-mother: games, fairs, contests and proclamations held in the last fortnight of summer, the season-feast that bears his name across Gaelic Ireland and Scotland.

sources.reference: Metrical Dindshenchas, 'Tailtiu'

irish_brigid.name: Imbolc, the early-spring feast of Brigid marking the start of lambing and the year's quickening
irish_brigid.notes: The goddess Brigit's name and patronage are continuous with the cult of St Brigit of Kildare at Imbolc/Lá Fhéile Bríde; the perpetual fire tended by nineteen women at Kildare is widely taken as a survival of her cult.

sources.reference: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998), s.v. Brigit / Imbolc

irish_tailtiu.name: the Áenach Tailten (Tailteann Games), funeral assembly held in her honour
irish_tailtiu.notes: By her dying wish Lugh founds games and a fair at Tailtiu (Teltown, Co. Meath); the assembly with its contests, matchmaking and proclamations continued in some form into the medieval period.

sources.reference: Metrical Dindshenchas, 'Tailtiu'

irish_donn.name: the gathering of the dead at Tech Duinn (the House of Donn, Bull Rock off Beara)
irish_donn.notes: A ninth-century poem has Donn declare that all his descendants shall come to his house after death; Tech Duinn on its sea-rock is the assembly-place of the Irish dead before their onward journey.

sources.reference: Dáithí Ó hÓgáin, Myth, Legend and Romance (1990), s.v. Donn / Tech Duinn

iroquois_handsome_lake.name: the Longhouse Religion (Gaiwiio), the renewed ceremonial cycle taught from his visions
iroquois_handsome_lake.cadence: seasonal cycle (Midwinter, Strawberry, Green Corn and Harvest thanksgivings)
iroquois_handsome_lake.notes: The Code of Handsome Lake is recited every other year at the longhouses; it knit his moral teaching to the old Haudenosaunee thanksgiving festivals, which continue among the Six Nations to this day.

sources.reference: Arthur C. Parker, The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913)

attributes.name: imagined as a powerful man crowned with caribou antlers, master of the herds
attributes.notes: Folk depictions show him as a robust hunter bearing caribou antlers, the sign of his dominion over the land-game.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tekkeitsertok'

sacredAnimals.name: the caribou (tuktu), the herds he owns and releases

sources.reference: Franz Boas, The Central Eskimo (1888)

attributes.name: the bright morning planet that rises ahead of the Sun
attributes.notes: Apisirahts is seen in the sky as the morning star, son of Sun (Natosi) and Moon (Ko'komiki'somm).

sources.reference: George Bird Grinnell, Blackfoot Lodge Tales (1892)

attributes.name: four birds that circle his head, said to be his kisses, carrying love between the young
attributes.notes: Late tradition figures the birds about Aengus's head as his kisses, messengers of the love he inspires.

sources.reference: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998), s.v. Óengus

sacredAnimals.name: the swan, the form he and Caer Ibormeith take to fly off together

sources.reference: Aislinge Óenguso (The Dream of Óengus)

attributes.name: a single vast eye in the back (or middle) of his head, lid raised on a ring by his attendants
attributes.notes: The poison eye, got from the fumes of his father's druids' brewing, withers and burns whatever its gaze falls on; it takes several men to heave up the heavy lid.

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

attributes.name: the Dark One, lord of a bleak sea-rock house, glimpsed riding the storm as a portent of death
attributes.notes: His name means 'the dark / brown one'; in folklore he rides on storm-clouds and his appearing foretells a death.

sources.reference: Dáithí Ó hÓgáin, Myth, Legend and Romance (1990), s.v. Donn

attributes.name: a proud warrior of surpassing beauty in a purple mantle, golden-yellow hair, bearing a five-pointed spear and a white-bossed shield set with gems
attributes.notes: Tochmarc Étaíne describes Midir as he appears to Eochaid: golden hair to his shoulders, lustrous eyes, a purple tunic, a gold-bossed shield and a sharp five-barbed spear.

sources.reference: Tochmarc Étaíne (The Wooing of Étaín)

sacredAnimals.name: the three cranes of churlishness that stand before his sídh, denying entry and hospitality

sources.reference: James MacKillop, Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (1998), s.v. Midir

sacredAnimals.name: the swan, the form he and Étaín take to escape from Tara

sources.reference: Tochmarc Étaíne (The Wooing of Étaín)

sacredPlants.name: the 365 healing herbs of Airmed, one for each sinew and joint of the body, that grew on Miach's grave

sources.reference: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Moytura)

sacredAnimals.name: the land of Ireland itself personified, met by the Milesians at the hill of Uisneach

sources.reference: Lebor Gabála Érenn

sacredPlants.name: the felled wood of Cúan turned to the harvest-plain of Brega, her labour and her grave

sources.reference: Metrical Dindshenchas, 'Tailtiu'

attributes.name: the Great White Pine with four white roots reaching to the four directions, the Tree of the Long Leaves
attributes.notes: Under the Tree of Peace the nations bury their weapons in the underground stream among its roots; an eagle is set atop to watch for danger.

sources.reference: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, The Great Law of Peace (Kaianerekowa)

sacredAnimals.name: the eagle perched atop the Tree of Peace, watcher against approaching enemies

sources.reference: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, The Great Law of Peace (Kaianerekowa)

sacredPlants.name: the white pine, whose five needles in a bundle figure the five united nations

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tree of Peace'

attributes.name: a body bent into seven crooks and a head of living snakes, straightened and combed at his conversion
attributes.notes: The image of Tadodaho before peace: monstrous, snake-haired, seven-times-crooked; Hayowentha combs the snakes from his hair, the act remembered in his name.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tadodaho'

attributes.name: clad in his own horn-skin, the hide no weapon could pierce, the hero of Áth Fhirdiad (Ardee)
attributes.notes: His invulnerable horn-skin is his defining attribute in the Táin; the ford where he fell, Áth Fhirdiad, is named for him.

sources.reference: Táin Bó Cúailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley)
